01.n: A masculine plural, 'all (persons)'. It stands first in the Greek sentence, ahead of its verb, as each object in this verse does.

02.r: Give every person the regard that is his due.
02.n: Abbott-Smith's first sense is 'to fix the value, price', then 'to honour'; it is the verb of τιμή, honour, in Romans 13:7 on this page. This first command is an aorist imperative; the three that follow are present imperatives.

03.r: A particular body: the community of believers.

04.n: Abbott-Smith gives an abstract sense, 'brotherly affection', and a concrete one, 'the brotherhood, the Christian community', under which he lists this verse. The Geneva's 'brotherly fellowship' leans toward the abstract sense.

05.r: Keep on showing goodwill and care to fellow believers.
05.n: Abbott-Smith defines the verb as 'to love, to feel and exhibit esteem and goodwill to a person'. A present imperative: an ongoing practice.

06.r: Greek puts the article before 'God'; English does not.

07.r: God, the one who alone is to be feared.

08.n: Abbott-Smith notes that in the New Testament the verb is always passive in form, 'to be seized with fear, be affrighted'. Fear is given to God alone in this verse, while the king receives 'honour', the same verb used for all people. Compare Romans 13:7, on this page, where fear stands among the things owed.

09.r: The particular king the readers live under.

10.r: The ruler over the readers, the Roman emperor.
10.n: Abbott-Smith notes that the word is used of the Roman Emperor, as often in common Greek, and cites this verse.

11.r: Give the king the regard owed to him.
11.n: The same verb as the first command of the verse, now as a present imperative. The king is to be honoured as all people are; the verse keeps the word 'fear' for God.
